n: Seeing the cloud, Solomon recalls that God had chosen to reveal Himself in thick darkness — as at Sinai. The cloud shows God is truly present, though veiled.
Solomon presents the temple to God as a permanent dwelling — a fixed home in place of the movable tabernacle.
Solomon turns from facing the temple to face the people and pronounces a blessing on them as they stand in respect.
Solomon praises God for keeping with His hands what He promised with His mouth. God’s word and deeds always match.

f.w: with his hands fulfilled that which he spake with his mouth

n: Solomon recounts God’s words: from the Exodus until David, God had not chosen one city for His temple or one permanent ruling family.

f.w: that my name might be there

n: But now God has chosen both Jerusalem as the place for His name and David to lead His people.
Solomon reminds the people that building a temple was David’s heartfelt desire.
God commended David for wanting to build the house. Even unfulfilled righteous desires are honored by God.

f.w: thou didst well in that it was in thine heart

n: Yet the work itself was given to David’s son. God sometimes lets one generation dream and another generation build.

f.g: From your own body — your direct descendant.

n: Solomon testifies that God has kept every part of His promise: Solomon sits on David’s throne and the temple stands.

f.g: In David’s place; as his successor.

n: The ark, holding the covenant tablets, now rests in the temple. The covenant is the heart of Israel’s relationship with God.
Solomon stands before the bronze altar in front of everyone and spreads out his hands — the ancient posture of prayer.

Solomon had built a bronze platform in the court. Standing on it, he knelt before all Israel with hands raised to heaven — a king humbling himself before the true King. This detail is unique to Chronicles.

f.g: A bronze platform, about 7½ feet square and 4½ feet high.

n: The dedicatory prayer begins: no god in heaven or earth is like the Lord, who keeps covenant and shows steadfast love to those who walk before Him wholeheartedly.
Solomon thanks God for keeping His word to David — promised by His mouth and fulfilled by His hand that very day.
Solomon asks God to keep the rest of the promise: David will always have an heir on the throne — on condition that his descendants obey God’s law.

f.w: There shall not fail thee a man

n: Solomon prays that God’s word to David will be proven true. Christians see its final fulfillment in Jesus, the eternal King from David’s line.
A profound question: can the infinite God really live among people on earth? Even the heavens can’t contain Him, let alone a building. The Gospel answers it: in Jesus, God dwelt among us.

f.w: will God in very deed dwell with men on the earth?

n: Solomon asks God to give attention to his prayer and pleading.
He asks that God’s eyes be on this house day and night and that He hear every prayer offered toward it. Ancient Israelites far away prayed facing the temple.
The theme of the whole prayer: when Your people pray here, hear from heaven — and forgive. The temple is above all a place of forgiveness.
The first case: when someone is accused of wronging a neighbor and must swear an oath of innocence before the altar.

f.w: an oath be laid upon him

n: Solomon asks God to judge justly in such cases — punishing the guilty and vindicating the innocent. God is the ultimate witness of truth.

f.w: recompensing his way upon his own head
f.g: Bringing his own conduct back on him.

n: Second case: when Israel is defeated in battle because of sin, yet turns back, confesses God, and prays in the temple.

f.g: Acknowledge God openly and His authority.

n: Then forgive them and bring them back to their land. Restoration follows repentance.

f.w: bring them again unto the land

n: Third case: drought sent because of sin. Rain in that dry land was life itself, and God had linked it to obedience.
Solomon asks God to forgive, teach His people the right way, and send rain. Forgiveness includes instruction for a better path.
Fourth: every kind of disaster — famine, plague, crop diseases, locusts, siege, or illness.

f.g: Crop damage from scorching east winds.

n: Whenever anyone, aware of his own sorrow, spreads out his hands toward this house, Solomon asks God to hear. Personal grief, not just national crisis, matters to God.

f.g: Feel his own affliction or the plague of his own heart.

n: Only God truly knows each heart, so only He can rightly forgive and repay each person according to his ways.
The purpose of God’s mercy is that His people will revere Him and walk in His ways all their lives.

f.g: Revere and honor God with awe.

n: Remarkably, Solomon also prays for foreigners who come because they’ve heard of God’s greatness. The temple was meant to bless all nations.

f.g: An image of God’s power displayed in delivering His people.

n: Grant the foreigner’s prayer, Solomon pleads, so that every nation may know and revere God and recognize this house as His.

f.w: that all people of the earth may know thy name

n: Next, when Israel goes to battle at God’s direction and prays toward Jerusalem and the temple.
Then hear and uphold their cause.

f.g: Secure justice for them; defend their right.

n: The last and longest case: when Israel sins — and everyone sins — and is carried into exile. Solomon is looking ahead to what would happen in Babylon.

f.w: there is no man which sinneth not

n: If in captivity they come to their senses and confess, “We have sinned, we have done wrong, we have acted wickedly.” Daniel prayed in this very spirit in Babylon.

f.g: Literally ‘bring back to their heart’ — come to their senses.

n: If they return to God with all their heart and soul and pray toward their land, city, and temple — full repentance, even far from home.

f.w: with all their heart and with all their soul

n: Then hear, defend them, and forgive. The Chronicler’s first readers, returned from exile, would have seen this prayer answered in their own story.
Solomon’s closing plea: let Your eyes be open and Your ears attentive to every prayer made here.
Quoting Psalm 132, Solomon invites God to arise and enter His resting place with the ark. He prays that priests be clothed with salvation and the faithful rejoice in God’s goodness.

f.w: arise, O LORD God, into thy resting place

n: Finally: do not reject Your anointed king; remember Your steadfast love for David. The prayer ends by resting on God’s covenant faithfulness.

f.g: Hebrew mashiaḥ — the anointed king; the root of the title Messiah.
